subject: maths
title: Chapter 9 · Test 1
summary: A 15-question test on Year 9 Chapter 9: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, shape of distributions, centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.
body:
This test covers Chapter 9, Probability and statistics: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, the shape of data distributions, measures of centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Show your working on paper.
- **Diagrams:** many questions have a histogram, table of outcomes or tree diagram — read the numbers on it carefully.
- **Levels:** 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge questions.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, go back to the lesson it came from and redo its worked examples. Then try another Chapter 9 test — each one has different questions on the same skills.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the lengths (cm) of 30 fish caught in a lake. How many fish were in the class 25 to less than 30 cm?
questions.explanation: The bar from 25 to 30 reaches a height of 6. The neighbouring bar (9) is for the next class.
steps: Find the bar that starts at 25 and ends at 30.
Read its height on the frequency axis: 6.

mistakes.B: Step 1: that is the bar for 30 to less than 35. Find the bar that starts at 25.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 25 is a class boundary on the horizontal axis. Read the bar’s height on the frequency axis.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 27 adds every bar from 25 upwards. Read just the one bar from 25 to 30.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the lengths (cm) of 30 fish caught in a lake, with class boundaries 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 and frequencies 3, 6, 9, 7, 4, 1

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the number of hours 45 people spent on social media in one day. Which word best describes the shape of the distribution?
questions.explanation: It is positively skewed: most values are low and a long tail stretches right, towards the larger values. Naming a skew after its peak instead of its tail is the usual slip.
steps: Look for the peak (or peaks) and for any long tail.
Here most values are low and a long tail stretches right, towards the larger values, so it is positively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the skew is named after the tail, not the peak. Here the long tail points right, to the larger values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: one side has a long low tail, so the two halves are not mirror images.
mistakes.D: Step 1: there is only one peak. Bimodal needs two clear peaks.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the number of hours 45 people spent on social media in one day, with class boundaries 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and frequencies 12, 14, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1

questions.prompt: The number of emails Kim received on 7 days: 9, 4, 13, 7, 2, 11, 10. What is the median?
questions.explanation: In order: 2, 4, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13. The middle (4th) value is 9. Taking the middle of the unordered list gives 7, which is wrong.
steps: 7 values, so the median is the 4th: 9.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 7 is the middle of the list as written. Put the values in order first.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 8 is the mean (total ÷ 7). The median is the middle value of the ordered list.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 11 is the range (13 − 2). The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: A six-sided die is rolled and a spinner with 5 equal sections is spun. How many different outcomes are there?
questions.explanation: Every one of the 6 outcomes of the first step can pair with every one of the 5 outcomes of the second: 6 × 5 = 30. Adding (11) misses most of the pairs.
steps: Step 1 has 6 outcomes and step 2 has 5.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added 6 + 5. Each of the 6 first results pairs with each of the 5 second results, so multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 6 counts only the die. Each die result can come with any of the 5 spinner results.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 5 × 5 uses the spinner twice. The die has 6 outcomes, not 5.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the number of minutes 50 students spent on homework one night. How many were 45 minutes or more?
questions.explanation: The bars from 45 upwards have heights 11 + 6 + 3 = 20. Using only the first of those bars (11) misses the rest.
steps: "45 or more" means every bar that starts at 45 or higher.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 11 is only the bar from 45 to 60. Every bar further right is also "45 or more".
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included the bar from 30 to 45. Start at the bar that begins at 45.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 30 counts the values LESS than 45. Add the bars from 45 upwards.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the number of minutes 50 students spent on homework one night, with class boundaries 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90 and frequencies 6, 10, 14, 11, 6, 3

questions.prompt: Eight runners’ lap times (seconds): 7, 4, 9, 16, 12, 15, 20, 25. Find the interquartile range.
questions.explanation: Ordered: 4, 7, 9, 12, 15, 16, 20, 25. Q1 = (7 + 9) ÷ 2 = 8 and Q3 = (16 + 20) ÷ 2 = 18, so IQR = 10. The range (21) uses the extremes instead.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 21 is the range (25 − 4). The IQR is Q3 − Q1.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 13.5 is the median of the whole set. The IQR is the difference between the quartiles.
mistakes.D: Step 2: each half has 4 values, so its median is the AVERAGE of its two middle values, not one of them.

questions.prompt: The table shows every sum when two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 9?
questions.explanation: Four of the 36 cells show 9 — (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3) — so P = 4/36 = 1/9. 1/11 wrongly treats every sum as equally likely.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the 11 sums (2 to 12) are not equally likely. Count the 36 equally likely cells.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there are 4 cells showing 9 — (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4), (6, 3). Count them all.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 9 can be made in more than one way. Count every cell showing 9.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 table showing the sums of two dice, from 2 in the top-left to 12 in the bottom-right

questions.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 5 white balls. A ball is taken, its colour noted, and it is put BACK. Then a second ball is taken. Use the tree diagram to find the probability that both balls are white.
questions.explanation: With replacement the branches stay the same, so P(WW) = 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64. 5/14 would be the answer without replacement.
steps: Follow the path W then W; with replacement both branches are 5/8.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 5/8 is only the first pick. Both must be white, so multiply by the second branch too.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the ball is put back, so the second pick is still 5 white out of 8, not 4 out of 7.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 3/8 × 5/8 is red then white. Follow the W–W path.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram with W 5/8 and R 3/8 at the first stage, and W 5/8 and R 3/8 again after each

questions.prompt: In a town, most people earn a moderate income, but a few people earn extremely high incomes. Which description of the income data is most likely correct?

options.A: Negatively skewed; the mean is greater than the median
options.B: Positively skewed; the mean is less than the median
options.C: Positively skewed; the mean is greater than the median
options.D: Symmetric; the mean equals the median

questions.explanation: A few very high incomes form a tail to the right (positive skew) and drag the mean above the median. Calling it negative names the shape after the pile, not the tail.
steps: The few extreme high values form a long tail to the right: positively skewed.
The tail pulls the mean towards it, so the mean is greater than the median.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the few very HIGH incomes form a tail to the right, which is positive skew.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the long right tail pulls the mean UP, above the median.
mistakes.D: Step 1: a few extreme high values make a long tail on one side, so it is not symmetric.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the breath-holding times (seconds) of 40 students. What percentage of them were less than 20 seconds?
questions.explanation: 3 + 7 = 10 out of 40, and 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%. Giving 10% forgets to divide by the total.
steps: Bars that are less than 20 seconds: 3 + 7 = 10.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you used only one bar (7). Include every bar that is less than 20 seconds.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 10 is the NUMBER of them. Divide by the total of 40 and multiply by 100.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included one bar too many. Check where "less than 20 seconds" starts and stops on the horizontal axis.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the breath-holding times (seconds) of 40 students, with class boundaries 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and frequencies 3, 7, 12, 10, 6, 2

questions.prompt: 6 test scores have a mean of 12. 5 of them are 10, 15, 9, 14, 11. What is the last one?
questions.explanation: All 6 must total 12 × 6 = 72; the known ones total 59, so the last is 72 − 59 = 13. Guessing it equals the mean is the common slip.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the missing value does not have to equal the mean. Use total = mean × number of values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there are 6 values, so the total is 12 × 6, not 12 × 5.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is the mean of the 5 known values. Find the total needed for all 6.

questions.prompt: A group has 5 girls and 3 boys. Two are chosen at random, one after the other, for two different jobs (no one gets both). Use the tree diagram to find the probability that both are boys.
questions.explanation: Along the boy–boy path: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28. 9/64 forgets that the first boy cannot be chosen again.
steps: Second choice (one boy gone, 7 left): P(boy) = 2/7.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 3/8 × 3/8 lets the same boy be chosen twice. After one boy is chosen, only 2 of the 7 left are boys.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the denominator 7 is right, but one boy has already been chosen, so only 2 boys are left, not 3.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 5/8 × 4/7 = 5/14 is both GIRLS. Follow the boy–boy path.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram for choosing two people without replacement: first G 5/8 and B 3/8; after G, G 4/7 and B 3/7; after B, G 5/7 and B 2/7; outcomes GG, GB, BG, BB

questions.prompt: A spinner has five equal sections numbered 1 to 5. It is spun twice. What is the probability of getting at least one 5?
questions.explanation: In the 25-cell table the 5-row and 5-column hold 5 + 5 − 1 = 9 cells (the (5, 5) cell is shared), so P = 9/25. Adding 1/5 + 1/5 counts (5, 5) twice.
steps: Make a 5 × 5 table: 25 equally likely outcomes.
Cells with a 5: 5 in the last row + 5 in the last column − 1 shared = 9.

mistakes.A: Step 2: adding 1/5 + 1/5 counts (5, 5) twice. Count the cells with at least one 5 in a 5 × 5 table.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you left out (5, 5). It has at least one 5 too.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 1/25 is the chance of TWO fives. "At least one" includes exactly one five as well.

questions.prompt: The mean of 9 numbers is 20. A tenth number is added and the mean becomes 21. What is the tenth number?
questions.explanation: Old total = 20 × 9 = 180; new total = 21 × 10 = 210; so the tenth number is 210 − 180 = 30.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the new number is not the new mean. Work out both totals and subtract.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 1 is how much the mean rose. Use totals: 21 × 10 and 20 × 9.
mistakes.D: Step 2: adding the two means does not give a data value. Find new total − old total.

questions.prompt: A bag has 12 counters, some red and the rest green. Two counters are drawn WITH replacement and P(both red) = 4/9. How many red counters are in the bag?
questions.explanation: With replacement P(both red) = P(red)², and 2/3 × 2/3 = 4/9, so P(red) = 2/3 and there are 2/3 × 12 = 8 red counters.
steps: With replacement, P(both red) = P(red) × P(red).

mistakes.A: Step 1: 4/9 is P(red) × P(red), not the fraction of red counters. Find the fraction that, squared, gives 4/9.
mistakes.C: Step 2: P(red) = 2/3, but you need 2/3 OF the 12 counters.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 4/9 × 12 uses the two-draw probability. Square-root it first to get P(red) for one draw.
